title: You are that, or you are his?
hookLine: a proud son comes home after twelve years of study, and his father gives him three words: tat tvam asi

lines: CLAY, A SEED, SALT IN WATER.
cards: A boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. At twenty-four, the Chandogya Upanishad says, he comes back proud, sure he's learned it all.
His father, Uddalaka, asks one question: did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown becomes known? The son has no idea.
So the father starts over, with a lump of clay, a seed, salt dissolved in water. And again and again he ends with three words: tat tvam asi.

teach.b: Tat tvam asi: you are that. Shankara's school hears it as the self and Brahman, not two. Five days ago you met Madhva's five differences.
Today, the reason underneath them. Madhva sorts everything that is into two kinds. One is svatantra, independent, depending on nothing.
Only God, Vishnu, is that. Everything else is paratantra, dependent: every soul, all of matter, even the goddess Lakshmi, his tradition says. All of it is real, and all of it leans on God.
His followers sum it up in a phrase: Hari sarvottama, Vishnu is supreme. So how does his school hear the father's three words?

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI, HEARD ANOTHER WAY.
teach.b: Some of its teachers hear tasya tvam asi, you are his: you belong to that.

teach.h: TASYA TVAM ASI: YOU ARE HIS.
teach.b: Others divide the sounds differently and hear atat tvam asi, you are not that. Same Sanskrit, a different ear. For Madhva, if the soul were secretly God, worship would be a kind of pretending.

teach.h: IF GOD IS OTHER, LOVE HAS A PLACE TO GO.
teach.b: If God is truly other, and the soul truly depends on him, then love has somewhere to go. Think back to Kanaka's window: a real distance, and a God who turns to cross it.
Advaita teachers would say the distance is finally unreal. Madhva's followers say it's where love lives. Both are Hindu, and both are still taught.
So when one Hindu says I am that, and another says I am his, they're quoting the same line.

how: Followers of Madhva, often called Madhvas, worship Vishnu as supreme; the Krishna temple at Udupi, which tradition says Madhva founded, is a center of their tradition, and pilgrims still look through Kanaka's window.

o: independent, depending on nothing: only God
free will, the soul's power to choose

games.q: Madhva's two kinds of real — tap the pairs.

s: for Madhva, the world is an illusion
Madhva taught that God, souls and the world are all real, and different forever.
in Madhva's thought, only God is independent
everything else, every soul, all matter, even Lakshmi, is real and depends on God.
Madhva's school reads tat tvam asi the same way Advaita does
its teachers hear 'you are his', or divide the sounds to hear 'you are not that'.

games.q: you're a teacher in Madhva's line. the Upanishad says tat tvam asi, 'you are that'. how does your school hear it?
o: the self and Brahman are one.
the soul belongs to God, and is not God.
the line is a copying mistake.
games.why: Madhva's school hears 'you are his', and some of its teachers divide the sounds as 'you are not that'. same Sanskrit, a different ear.

practice: Let yourself feel small for a moment, in a good way: not ashamed, just small, the way you feel under a big sky, with so much bigger than you, the day ahead, the people you love, whatever holds it all.
Let the distance be fine; Kanakadasa sang from outside the wall. If you pray, turn toward God from exactly where you are; if you don't, face toward something larger, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Svatantra, independent, depending on nothing. Only God is svatantra; souls and the world are real, different, and depend on him. The distance isn't a problem to solve. It's where love goes.

orig.note: Sanskrit: self-ruled, independent. in Madhva's thought only God is svatantra; everything else is paratantra, dependent.

carryVoice: Your line: svatantra, only God is independent. Everything else leans on him. That's day two ninety-three.

sources.ref: Madhva's division of reality into svatantra and paratantra, and the five differences (pancha-bheda), as taught in the Madhva tradition
